name: Supply Voltage (120 VAC)
purpose: Verify correct line voltage at outlet or terminal block before troubleshooting downstream components.
failureModes: Low voltage causes weak compressor start, dim lights, motor hum
No voltage indicates upstream supply issue (breaker, outlet, cord)
High voltage can indicate wiring fault or wrong circuit
testingTips: Measure at outlet behind unit, not through an extension cord
Check under load (unit running) vs. no-load for voltage drop

name: Supply Voltage (240 VAC)
purpose: Verify correct line-to-line voltage for 240V appliances before assuming component failure.
failureModes: Low voltage causes slow heat-up (dryer/range), long cycle times
Single-leg voltage (~120V present, ~240V absent) indicates open leg/breaker/blown fuse
No voltage indicates upstream supply issue
testingTips: Check L1-L2, L1-N, and L2-N separately to isolate a single open leg
Verify at the outlet/junction box, not just at the appliance terminal block

name: Freezer Cabinet Temperature
purpose: Confirm freezer compartment is holding manufacturer target temp (industry target ~0°F).
failureModes: High temp: sealed system issue, poor door seal, iced evaporator, low charge
Extremely low/erratic: thermostat/control board fault
testingTips: Use a thermometer between packages, not on an air vent
Allow 24 hrs after door open/reset before trusting reading
notes: Verify against specific model's target setpoint when available

name: Fresh Food Cabinet Temperature
purpose: Confirm fresh food compartment holds manufacturer target temp (industry target ~37°F).
failureModes: High temp: damper/air handling fault, weak seal, sealed system issue
Below freezing: damper stuck open, thermistor/control fault
testingTips: Use a thermometer at mid-shelf height, away from vents
Give reading time to stabilize after door activity
notes: Verify against specific model's target setpoint when available

name: Ambient Room Temperature
purpose: Establish install-environment baseline; out-of-range ambient affects cooling/heating performance and can mimic a component fault.
failureModes: Garage/basement install below normal ambient can cause fridge/freezer control issues
Excess ambient heat load (near oven, direct sun, poor ventilation) drives run times up on refrigeration
testingTips: Measure a few feet from the unit, not right against a heat source or vent

name: Defrost Heater Resistance
purpose: Verify defrost heater continuity and resistance value to rule out open or shorted element.
failureModes: Open (OL) = no defrost heat, frost buildup on evaporator
Reading well outside range = shorted/damaged element or wrong part
testingTips: Disconnect power and unplug heater leads before testing
Compare reading against nameplate wattage using Ohm's law if spec unknown (R = V²/W)
notes: Verify model spec — wattage varies significantly by cabinet size (typically 300-600W on 120-240V)

name: Defrost Thermostat / Bi-Metal Continuity
purpose: Verify defrost terminator closes at frosted/cold evaporator temp so the heater can energize.
failureModes: Open (OL) at frosted evaporator: failed terminator — heater circuit never completes
High resistance: poor contacts or failing bi-metal switch
testingTips: Test at the connector with power disconnected
Best checked when evaporator is frosted/cold — terminator should be closed (near 0 Ω); opens when warm after defrost
notes: Some models use electronic adaptive defrost with no bi-metal — skip if not equipped

name: Defrost Thermal Fuse Continuity
purpose: Verify defrost thermal fuse continuity — an open fuse blocks defrost heat permanently.
failureModes: Open (OL): blown thermal fuse — no defrost heat
Often caused by failed heater, stuck relay, or prior overheating event
testingTips: Disconnect power before testing at fuse terminals
If blown, inspect heater and wiring for cause before replacing fuse only
notes: Not all models have an inline defrost fuse — OL may mean not equipped or open circuit upstream

name: Compressor Run Amperage
purpose: Confirm compressor is drawing expected run current after startup, ruling out locked rotor or refrigerant/mechanical issues.
failureModes: High amps: locked/dragging compressor, high head pressure, overcharge
Low/zero amps after start attempt: start relay/capacitor fault, open winding, tripped overload
testingTips: Use clamp meter on common wire; measure after startup surge settles (a few seconds in)
Compare to nameplate FLA/RLA rating on compressor when readable
notes: Verify against compressor nameplate rating — varies by model and compressor size

name: Compressor Run Winding Resistance
purpose: Verify compressor run/start winding continuity and rule out open or shorted winding.
failureModes: Open (OL) on any winding pair = failed compressor
Very low reading (near 0) between winding and case = grounded/shorted winding
testingTips: Test C-S, C-R, S-R at compressor terminals with power disconnected
S-R should roughly equal C-S + C-R; large mismatch suggests bad winding
Also megohm-test winding to case for ground fault
notes: Verify against compressor nameplate/spec sheet — varies widely by compressor model

name: Condenser Fan Motor Amperage
purpose: Confirm condenser fan motor is running and drawing normal current for adequate condenser airflow.
failureModes: Zero amps: seized bearing, open winding, failed start circuit
High amps: motor dragging/binding on debris or failing bearing
testingTips: Clamp on motor common lead with unit running in cooling cycle
Check for physical obstruction/dust buildup before condemning motor
notes: Verify against motor nameplate rating when available

name: Evaporator Fan Motor Amperage
purpose: Confirm evaporator fan motor is circulating air across the coil into the cabinet.
failureModes: Zero amps: seized motor, open winding, failed door switch signal (on models with door-off fan cutoff)
High amps: fan blade iced up/obstructed, motor bearing failure
testingTips: Check that door switch isn't preventing fan operation during test
Inspect for ice buildup on blade from prior defrost failure before condemning motor
notes: Verify against motor nameplate rating when available

name: Cabinet Thermistor Resistance
purpose: Verify thermistor resistance at known ambient/cabinet temp to rule out sensor drift or failure.
failureModes: Open (OL): sensor failure, wiring break — often triggers error code or default temp behavior
Shorted (near 0): sensor failure — often triggers different error code
testingTips: Test at room temp for a rough sanity check; for precision, test at a known temp (ice water ~32°F) against manufacturer's resistance table
Resistance drops as temp rises (NTC behavior) — direction of drift matters, not just magnitude
notes: Many models ~0.2 Ω ±0.1 at room temp — verify against manufacturer's temp/resistance table when known; values vary meaningfully by brand and sensor type

name: Electric Dryer Supply Amperage
purpose: Confirm dryer is drawing expected current on its dedicated 30A circuit during heat cycle.
failureModes: At/near 30A sustained: circuit near capacity, check for undersized wire/breaker nuisance tripping
Low/no amps on heat call: open heating element, thermal fuse/limit open, control relay fault
testingTips: Clamp each hot leg separately during an active heat call, not just tumble/no-heat
Confirm breaker/circuit is actually rated 30A before flagging as abnormal
notes: Assumes standard 30A dedicated dryer circuit context — verify circuit rating on install

name: Electric Range Supply Amperage
purpose: Confirm range is drawing expected current on its dedicated 50A circuit during bake/broil/surface element use.
failureModes: At/near 50A sustained across multiple elements: circuit near capacity, expected under heavy multi-element load
Low/no amps on a single element call: open element, faulty infinite switch/relay, wiring fault at that element only
testingTips: Test one element/function at a time to isolate which circuit is drawing incorrectly
Confirm breaker/circuit is actually rated 50A before flagging as abnormal
notes: Assumes standard 50A dedicated range circuit context — verify circuit rating on install
